14120-answer-to-dr-priestley-s-letters-t:
Attributed to Matthew Turner and William Hammon, this 1782 answer takes up Dr. Priestley's Letters to a Philosophical Unbeliever. The editor states his aim plainly: to answer Priestley rather than preach natural religion, and to ask whether reason proves a deity and his attributes at all. Revealed knowledge stays aside, so Christians need take no offense at the inquiry.

Analogy bears the attack. Priestley argues from makers to a maker, but Hammon replies that whoever first made a chair must have grasped its use, while nature's works arise by generation and vegetation, not by craft. Hume's point follows: a table and the world differ too much for one to prove the other. Few inquirers, the writer adds, can give tolerable grounds for belief, and learned men disagree on every proof. Cool, candid, and skeptical, the pamphlet stands as early English freethought in action.
17857-forgotten-books-of-the-american-nu:
Rosalie V. Halsey wrote Forgotten Books of the American Nursery in 1911, printed in Boston by Charles E. Goodspeed in a run of seven hundred copies. Halsey traces how the American story-book grew, from English play-books to the toy-books of the early 1800s.

Chapters move from Newbery's books in America to patriotic printers, the child and his book at the close of the 1700s, and the cheap toy-books that followed. Halsey writes with charm and care for old bindings, pictures, and texts. It is a delightful history for book lovers, and a guide to the nursery shelves of early America.
20505-what-s-in-the-new-york-evening-jou:
What's in the New York Evening Journal?, published in 1928, is a promotional book about William Randolph Hearst's great evening paper. It calls the Journal America's greatest evening newspaper. The book walks readers through its news, features, and comics.

Its star attraction was Arthur Brisbane, who wrote editorials for the paper for many years. His daily editorials, the book boasts, were one of the outstanding reasons nearly half of all New York newspaper buyers chose the Evening Journal. The volume is a period piece of press ballyhoo, showing how mass papers sold themselves.
22586-history-of-the-second-massachusett:
History of the Second Massachusetts Regiment of Infantry is a regimental history of a Union Civil War unit, written from the memories of its officers. The catalog record names no single author and gives no year. Such histories were often read at veterans' gatherings, and the text keeps the warm, spoken tone of a reunion address.

The sample recalls camp life shared with the Third Wisconsin and a mess run by a caterer named Charley Johnson and his staff. It also marks the departure of Colonel Shaw, then a captain in the regiment, who left to lead the famed Fifty-fourth Massachusetts, the celebrated Black regiment. The book preserves small human details that official reports omit. It suits readers tracing the daily life of a fighting regiment.
31303-euphorion-vol-i-being-studies-of-t:
Vernon Lee's Euphorion, volume one, dedicated to Walter Pater, studies the antique and the medieval in the Renaissance. Its introduction takes Goethe's Euphorion, the marvelous child of Faust and Helena, as the spirit of the modern world, born of the mystic marriage between medieval yearning and recovered Greek beauty. Lee borrows that reading from Symonds's Renaissance in Italy.

Faust himself appears as an old scholar whose postponed youth boils with appetites, curiosities, and mad visions of unreal worlds, mocked by dreams of superhuman power. Through such figures, Lee traces how the Middle Ages took Helen to wife and what their offspring became, in essays of rare learning and imagination.
31605-the-cooking-manual-of-practical-di:
Juliet Corson, superintendent of the New York Cooking School, published The Cooking Manual of Practical Directions for Economical Every-Day Cookery at New York with Dodd, Mead, and Company in 1877. Its motto asks how well people can live if they are moderately poor. The preface states the book's aim plainly, for housekeepers and cooks who want the healthiest, tastiest dishes for the lowest cost.

Corson's manual runs in fourteen chapters and more, covering the daily work of an economical kitchen. It teaches thrift as a skill, not as hardship, and it treats good cooking as a matter of method, choice of materials, and care in the kitchen.
33336-the-welsh-and-their-literature-fro:
George Borrow's Welsh and Their Literature, taken from the London Quarterly Review of 1861, surveys Wales and its letters in a short, sharp essay. Borrow opens with the Welsh calling themselves Cymry, and he takes up The Sleeping Bard, or Visions of the World, Death, and Hell, by Elis Wyn, translated by Borrow himself in 1860. His essay weighs Welsh style, spirit, and story.

The piece suits readers of Celtic literature and of Borrow, whose love of languages and roads shines through. Its tone is bold and personal, as Borrow judges books with a traveler's eye. For students of Welsh writing, it is a lively, mid-Victorian introduction to a literature too little known in England.
33828-abbreviations-and-signs-a-primer-o:
Frederick W. Hamilton, education director for the United Typothetae of America, wrote this 1918 primer for printing apprentices. It gives rules for abbreviations and classified lists of those in most common use: dates, time, place names, titles, book sizes, weights, and measures. Later lists cover money, maths, medicine, stars, church, and proofreaders' signs.

Hamilton urges printers to spell words out in full wherever room allows, and to shorten only by rule. Review questions and further reading close the primer. The book is a useful window on the print shop of its day, and a handy key to old books full of short forms.
8305-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-05-deut:
Deuteronomy is the fifth book of the Douay-Rheims Bible, in Bishop Challoner's revision of the Catholic text translated from the Latin Vulgate. It presents Moses, at the end of his life, speaking to a new generation of Israelites camped east of the Jordan. He retells the law, recalls the journey from Egypt, and sets before the people a choice between blessing and curse.

The book repeats much of Exodus and Numbers, but with a preacher's urgency, and it closes with Moses viewing the promised land he will not enter, then dying. Its great command, to love God with all heart, soul, and strength, stands at the center of Jewish prayer to this day. Challoner's text gives it in stately, older English.
8345-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-45-1-ma:
When a Greek king tried to stamp out Jewish worship, a priest's family took up arms, and 1 Machabees tells their revolt. Mattathias refuses the king's sacrifice, his son Judas, called Machabeus, wins stunning victories with a small force, and the temple is cleansed and rededicated, the origin of Hanukkah. The book follows the brothers through battles, treaties with Rome, and the founding of a free Jewish state.

Written as sober history, with speeches and documents, it is the best source for the Maccabean revolt. The book belongs to the Catholic canon, and Challoner's Douay-Rheims text gives it in Vulgate-based English. Readers meet guerrilla war, diplomacy, and faith under an empire, told without miracles softening the cost.
8346-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-46-2-ma:
Where 1 Machabees tells the revolt as sober history, 2 Machabees retells it as a story of martyrs and miracles. The book opens with letters urging Jews in Egypt to keep Hanukkah. It then follows Judas Machabeus through battles, and lingers on the mother and seven sons tortured for refusing to eat forbidden food. Their deaths, and the promise of resurrection, anchor the book's theology.

A second martyr tale, the old scribe Eleazar, and prayers for the dead, which later readers linked to purgatory, fill the middle. The book belongs to the Catholic canon, and Challoner's Douay-Rheims text gives it in Vulgate-based English. It is history written to stiffen courage under persecution, with wonders left in full view.
8357-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-57-phil:
Philippians is Paul's happiest letter, written from prison to the church in Philippi, the first he founded in Europe. He thanks them for a gift, urges two quarreling women to agree, and sets out the hymn of Christ who emptied himself, took a servant's form, and was raised high. Joy recurs on nearly every page, even as Paul faces possible death.

Warnings against rival teachers and a closing note of contentment, learning to live with plenty or want, round out the short letter. In Challoner's Douay-Rheims wording, Paul's warmth keeps an older, formal tone. Readers return to Philippians for its balance: deep feeling held by clear teaching, and joy chosen rather than merely felt.
answer-to-dr-priestley-s-letters-to-a-ph: William Hammon answers Dr. Priestley's letters to a philosophical unbeliever, in part one published in London in 1782, with advertisement and prefatory address. The reply defends belief against Priestley's rationalist arguments, point by point. Hammon's pamphlet records a lively corner of Enlightenment religious debate. The tone stays firm, yet never loses courtesy.
britannica-1911-berdichev:
Berdichev is a town of western Russia, in the government of Kiev, 116 miles south-west of the city of Kiev by rail. Its chief church is the cathedral of the Assumption, finished in 1832. A fortified Carmelite monastery, founded in 1627, was taken and plundered by the Cossack leader Chmielnicki in 1647 and shut down in 1864.

Trade is the town’s life: peltry, silk goods, iron and wooden wares, salt fish, grain, cattle and horses all pass through its market. Four fairs meet yearly, the greatest on 12 June and 15 August. Tobacco, soap, candles, oil, bricks and leather are made locally. Its people numbered 53,728 in 1897, about eighty per cent of them Jews.
doe-osti-2999065-near-term-reliability-a:
Samuel Ojetola and David Schoenwald of Sandia National Laboratories revisit how the electric grid's strength is measured, in report SAND2025-13069, printed September 2025. Utilities quote reliability figures every year, yet big storms and attacks test something broader: resilience, the ability to bend, degrade and recover. The report argues the two ideas need distinct, well-chosen measures, especially for near-term planning.

An event is traced through five phases, from quiet running through disturbance, weakened operation, repair, and the state after repair. Standard reliability metrics then get a fresh look, among them planning reserve margin and loss of load probability. Each measure is weighed for what it truly captures about an event as it unfolds over time. The aim is a metric set that grid planners can apply now, before the next large disturbance, rather than a score settled only after the fact.
doe-osti-3008383-modal-analysis-and-test:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2014193, by Kaden Foster, dated December 2025, is both a results report and a how-to guide for modal analysis of a cantilever beam. Modal analysis finds the natural vibration frequencies and shapes of a part, the modes it will ring at when struck.

The guide walks the full loop: simulate first, then test, analyze, and feed the lessons back into the design until it satisfies. Finite element modelling in ANSYS lets the beam's model be refined quickly, with mesh density and degrees of freedom setting the model's fidelity. A beam fixed at one end is the classic teaching case, and this walkthrough gives new analysts a checked example to learn the process on.
doe-osti-3020009-em-influence-of-nanocon:
Final report for DOE award DE-SC0021389, from a University of California, Riverside project led by Younjin Min, studies how tiny mineral grains underground carry pollutants with them. Energy work leaves organic and inorganic waste in rock layers. These attach to submicron grains called geocolloids, which move through cracks only nanometers to micrometers wide. Heat and tight confinement change how the particles travel.

Using a Surface Forces Apparatus plus several microscopy and spectroscopy tools, the team gauged the forces between confined grains. Electrostatic double-layer forces controlled the behavior, with Debye lengths of about 20 to 24 nanometers, matching theory. Under confinement the mixes shifted from free-flowing to solid-like flow. At salt levels of 10 to 100 millimolar potassium chloride, the particles jammed into fixed networks that water flow could not easily move.
doe-osti-3020492-high-waste-loading-glas:
Vitreous State Laboratory final report VSL-17R3700-1, by Keith S. Matlack, Wing K. Kot, and Ian L. Pegg of The Catholic University of America, develops glass recipes for one of Hanford's harder waste streams: high-level waste rich in phosphorus. Published in May 2017 and released under HFO-73167, the work serves the Hanford Tank Waste Treatment and Immobilization Plant. Higher waste loading in glass means fewer canisters to fill, store, and bury.

Phosphorus tends to separate out of molten glass, so loading has limits. The team made simulant feeds, melted trial glasses, and measured their properties, including how much phosphate crystallized during heat treatment at 950 degrees Celsius for 70 hours. One formulation reached 51 percent waste loading with a real waste batch composition. Leach testing checked that the glasses still met environmental limits.
doe-osti-3020569-high-waste-loading-glas:
Vitreous State Laboratory final report VSL-17R4120-1 (Rev. 1), by Keith S. Matlack, Hao Gan, Wing K. Kot, and Ian L. Pegg of The Catholic University of America, develops glass formulations for Hanford high-level waste rich in manganese. Published in December 2017 and released under HFO-73169, the work supports turning tank waste into borosilicate glass at the Hanford Tank Waste Treatment and Immobilization Plant. Packing more waste into each batch of glass reduces the total number of canisters.

Manganese-rich waste changes how glass melts and flows, so recipes must be tuned and proven at laboratory scale. The team prepared simulant feeds across a matrix of compositions, melted trial glasses, and measured properties such as viscosity and composition by X-ray fluorescence. The data identify formulations that carry high waste loading while staying within the plant's processing limits.
doe-osti-3363381-megawatt-and-electrolyz: Big hydrogen machines scaled to megawatt size got their DOE capability check, and this CRADA final signs off the electrolyzers. The pages detail the results. The energy folks get their closeout. The check was size. The closeout were energy. The energy were folks.
doe-osti-3369036-2025-cea-smad-digitizer: CEA SMAD got 2025-approved, and this DOE evaluation covers digitizer type. The pages detail the findings. The engineers get their data. The approval was type. The data were engineer. The SMAD were CEA. The 2025 were evaluation. The engineers were data.
doe-osti-3376842-from-war-to-work-risks-: Coming home from deployment is its own battle — jobs, family, and health all shift at once. Noonan and Porter's report maps the risks and challenges across the full deployment cycle, from send-off to return. It pairs each challenge with evidence-based strategies that actually help veterans land on their feet.
doe-osti-3377465-cyber-informed-engineer: CIE got standards-quick-started, and this DOE guide covers quick starts. The pages detail the development findings. The security folks get their data. The organization was standards. The data were security. The CIE were guide. The quick were start.
forgotten-books-of-the-american-nursery-:
Halsey traces the American story-book from English play-books to the first native children's tales. Her chapters cover Newbery's books in America and the cheap chapbooks that followed them. Isaiah Thomas and other early printers spread the little volumes through the young republic.

One detail shows the trade's thrift. The Death and Burial of Cock Robin survives in a red and gilt cover stamped from dies first cut for German playing-cards. The single word Münch in one corner marks the paper as made in Germany. Rosalie V. Halsey published this history in Boston in 1911, in an edition of seven hundred copies.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-InternalRevenue:
Floyd David Moore, chief of the IRS Intelligence Division's New Orleans district, swore an affidavit about a meeting held on May 29, 1969. His visitor was Pershing Gervais, the former Garrison investigator. The subject of their talk was payoffs to Louisiana public officials.

An affidavit from a tax intelligence chief is a serious paper: sworn, specific, and filed for use. Gervais moved between the district attorney's office and the underworld it investigated, and a meeting about payoffs put him on the federal record. Moore's statement preserves that meeting as the IRS chief swore it happened.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, died in 2022, and the Archive published this memorial. Its opening line is unsparing about his country after him. Gorbachev ended the Cold War, only to see party apparatchiks destroy his country, a process the posting says continues.

The memorial's second claim fits the Archive's mission: Gorbachev made history, then freed history by opening his documents. Few leaders have given archivists more. His papers and his foundation's records underpin many of the Archive's Russia publications. An institution built on documents marking his death in those terms is both tribute and a fair statement of his documentary legacy.

Before NATO enlarged eastward, Western leaders spoke with Mikhail Gorbachev about the alliance's future as Germany reunified. What he was told, and whether it amounted to a promise, became a lasting dispute. This briefing-book page presents the record of what Gorbachev heard. Its companion volume covers what Boris Yeltsin heard later in the decade. The evidence here is the title alone. Read together, the two volumes let readers compare the assurances themselves rather than the claims made about them.

Anatoly Chernyaev, the Soviet aide whose diaries became one of the great insider sources on the Cold War's end, was born in 1921. The National Security Archive marked his centennial, the hundredth anniversary of his birth, with a briefing book page honoring the man and the record he left behind. Chernyaev served Mikhail Gorbachev and wrote down what he saw. Only the page capture survives in this entry's evidence, but its subject is the diarist, celebrated by the institution that has spent years publishing his work in English.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-05-deuterono:
Deuteronomy, in Douay-Rheims English, translated out of the Latin Vulgate and later revised by Bishop Richard Challoner (1749-1752). The Old Testament first came from Douay, in 1609 and 1610; the New Testament from Rheims, in 1582. Chapter one begins beyond the Jordan, in a plain wilderness facing the Red Sea, between Pharan, Thophel, Laban, and Haseroth.

Moses speaks to all Israel, repeating what passed at Sinai and at Cadesbarne. A heading recalls the people's murmuring and their punishment. The distance from Horeb by way of Mount Seir is given as eleven days' journey. A second telling of the law, spoken on the edge of a new land, is the book's plain frame: memory, warning, and command joined together.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-45-1-machabe:
First Machabees, in Douay-Rheims wording, Englished from the Latin Vulgate and revised under Bishop Richard Challoner, 1749 to 1752. Rheims printed the New Testament in 1582; Douay printed the Old Testament in 1609 and 1610. An introduction argues for its authority, citing Augustine and the councils of Florence and Trent. Though not received by the Jews, it says, the church received it by apostolic tradition.

Chapter one then turns to the Greek world that pressed on Judea, in the fuller text behind the heading. Wars, a temple profaned, and brothers who resist form the history that follows. Readers meet a family-led revolt told as sacred history, with the canon question answered before the narrative begins.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-46-2-machabe:
Second Machabees, in the Douay-Rheims version, made from the Latin Vulgate and reworked by Bishop Richard Challoner between 1749 and 1752. Behind it stand a Rheims New Testament of 1582 and a Douay Old Testament of 1609 and 1610. An introduction calls it a short abstract, in Greek, of five volumes by Jason of Cyrene about Judas and his brethren.

It begins with two letters from the Jews of Jerusalem to their brethren in Egypt. Chapter one's heading gives thanks for delivery from Antiochus. The letters urge keeping the feast of the dedication of the altar and of a miraculous fire. Letters first, then history: this book frames revolt as worship defended and remembered in festival.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-57-philippia:
Philippians, in Douay-Rheims wording, Englished from the Latin Vulgate and revised under Bishop Richard Challoner, 1749 to 1752. Rheims printed the New Testament in 1582; Douay printed the Old Testament in 1609 and 1610. An introduction notes Paul's thanks to the Philippians for their gifts to him. It dates the letter to about twenty-nine years after the Ascension.

Chapter one is headed simply as the apostle's affection for the Philippians. Paul and Timothy write as servants of Christ to all the saints at Philippi, with bishops and deacons. Grace and peace open a warm letter. Gratitude and partnership, rather than rebuke, set its tone, even though Paul writes as a prisoner in the wider letter.
